name: Aortic Stenosis
tagline: Progressive narrowing of the aortic valve orifice, imposing a chronic pressure load on the left ventricle and, once symptomatic, carrying a poor prognosis without intervention.
overview: Aortic stenosis is the commonest valve lesion requiring intervention in high-income countries. In older adults it is usually caused by calcific degenerative disease, an active process resembling atherosclerosis rather than passive wear. A congenitally bicuspid valve — present in roughly 1–2% of people — undergoes the same process earlier, typically presenting one to two decades sooner. Rheumatic disease remains a major cause worldwide. The obstruction develops over years, and the left ventricle compensates by concentric hypertrophy. Patients remain asymptomatic for a long time, but the onset of angina, syncope or heart failure marks a sharp change in prognosis and is the trigger for intervention.

modifiable: Hypertension
Dyslipidaemia, particularly elevated lipoprotein(a)
Smoking
Diabetes mellitus
Chronic kidney disease and disordered calcium–phosphate metabolism
nonModifiable: Genetic factors including lipoprotein(a) locus variants

pathophysiology.title: Endothelial injury and lipid entry
pathophysiology.text: Mechanical stress, greatest on the aortic side of the cusps, damages the valvular endothelium. Lipoproteins enter the leaflet and are oxidatively modified.

pathophysiology.title: Inflammation
pathophysiology.text: Macrophages and T lymphocytes infiltrate the leaflet, releasing cytokines that sustain a chronic inflammatory process — this is an active biology, not simple wear and tear.

pathophysiology.title: Osteogenic transformation
pathophysiology.text: Valvular interstitial cells differentiate into an osteoblast-like phenotype, laying down calcium hydroxyapatite within the leaflet. Fibrosis and neovascularisation accompany this.

pathophysiology.title: Leaflet thickening and reduced excursion
pathophysiology.text: Progressive calcification stiffens the cusps and restricts their opening. Unlike rheumatic disease, degenerative calcific stenosis characteristically spares the commissures.

pathophysiology.title: Rising pressure gradient
pathophysiology.text: As the effective orifice area falls, a systolic pressure gradient develops between ventricle and aorta. Velocity across the valve rises, and the ventricle must generate progressively higher pressures.

pathophysiology.title: Concentric hypertrophy
pathophysiology.text: By Laplace's law, the ventricle adds sarcomeres in parallel to normalise wall stress. This preserves ejection fraction and stroke volume for years — the compensated phase.

pathophysiology.title: Diastolic dysfunction
pathophysiology.text: The hypertrophied, fibrotic ventricle relaxes poorly. Filling pressures rise, and the atrial contribution to filling becomes critical — which is why atrial fibrillation is poorly tolerated.

pathophysiology.title: Supply–demand mismatch
pathophysiology.text: Hypertrophied muscle has increased oxygen demand, while raised end-diastolic pressure and shortened diastole reduce coronary perfusion pressure. Subendocardial ischaemia causes angina even with normal coronary arteries.

pathophysiology.title: Decompensation
pathophysiology.text: Eventually the ventricle can no longer sustain the load. Afterload mismatch and fibrosis reduce ejection fraction, cardiac output falls, and symptoms of heart failure appear. Once symptomatic, survival without intervention is markedly reduced.

anatomyInvolved: Aortic valve cusps and annulus
Left ventricular outflow tract
Left ventricular myocardium, which hypertrophies concentrically
Coronary circulation, compromised by raised filling pressure and hypertrophy
Ascending aorta, which may show post-stenotic dilatation or bicuspid aortopathy
Conduction system, lying immediately beneath the valve
physiologyChanges: Increased left ventricular systolic pressure with a transvalvular gradient
Concentric hypertrophy with increased wall thickness and reduced compliance
Elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and impaired relaxation
Reduced coronary perfusion pressure with subendocardial ischaemia
Fixed stroke volume that cannot increase appropriately with exertion
Delayed and diminished carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a narrow pulse pressure
In low-flow states, a low gradient despite severe stenosis — the pitfall of low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis

progression.text: Leaflet thickening without significant obstruction. A marker of cardiovascular risk; a minority progress to stenosis.
Measurable gradient with preserved valve area. Usually asymptomatic; requires surveillance.
Valve area under 1.0 cm², mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more, with no symptoms. Careful follow-up and exercise testing to unmask symptoms.
Angina, syncope or heart failure appear. Prognosis deteriorates sharply and intervention is indicated.
Reduced ejection fraction, pulmonary hypertension and low cardiac output; higher procedural risk and worse outcomes.

symptoms: Exertional breathlessness — usually the earliest symptom
Exertional angina, often with unobstructed coronary arteries
Exertional syncope or presyncope, from a fixed stroke volume with exercise-induced vasodilatation
Reduced exercise tolerance and fatigue
Symptoms of heart failure in advanced disease
Patients frequently under-report, having gradually reduced their activity
signs: Ejection systolic murmur, loudest in the second right intercostal space, radiating to the carotids
Slow-rising, low-volume carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a narrow pulse pressure
Soft or absent aortic component of the second heart sound in severe disease
Sustained, non-displaced apex beat from concentric hypertrophy
Fourth heart sound reflecting a stiff ventricle
Reversed splitting of the second heart sound in severe disease
The murmur may become quieter as stenosis becomes critical and stroke volume falls

investigations.findings: The key test — peak velocity, mean gradient, valve area by continuity equation, leaflet morphology, ventricular hypertrophy and function.
Distinguishes true severe stenosis from pseudo-severe stenosis in low-flow, low-gradient disease with reduced ejection fraction.
Aortic valve calcium scoring supports severity assessment in equivocal cases, and provides annular sizing and vascular access assessment before intervention.
Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern; conduction abnormalities are common.
In asymptomatic severe stenosis, performed under supervision to unmask symptoms or an abnormal blood pressure response. Contraindicated in symptomatic patients.
Rising levels may indicate ventricular decompensation and help in the timing of intervention.
Angiography or CT before intervention, since concomitant coronary disease is common.

complications: Sudden cardiac death, particularly once symptoms have developed
Atrial fibrillation, poorly tolerated because of dependence on the atrial kick
Conduction disease and heart block, especially after intervention
Acquired von Willebrand syndrome with angiodysplastic gastrointestinal bleeding (Heyde's syndrome)

treatment.principles: There is no medical therapy that halts progression; the definitive treatment is valve replacement. Timing rests principally on the development of symptoms and on evidence of ventricular decompensation. The choice between surgical and transcatheter replacement is made by a multidisciplinary heart team considering age, anatomy, comorbidity and patient preference. Educational summary only — decisions must follow current guidelines and individual assessment.

groups.name: Surveillance
groups.detail: Serial echocardiography at intervals determined by severity, with patient education on the symptoms that should prompt urgent review.

groups.name: Risk factor management
groups.detail: Treatment of hypertension and cardiovascular risk factors; statins have not been shown to slow stenosis progression.

groups.name: Surgical aortic valve replacement
groups.detail: Mechanical or bioprosthetic valves; the established option, particularly in younger patients and where concomitant surgery is needed.

groups.name: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation
groups.detail: Now used across a broad risk spectrum, with the decision informed by age, anatomy and life expectancy.

groups.name: Balloon valvuloplasty
groups.detail: A bridging or palliative measure in selected patients; restenosis is rapid.

groups.name: Careful haemodynamic management
groups.detail: Caution with vasodilators and any cause of hypotension in severe stenosis, since stroke volume cannot increase to compensate.

keyTakeaways: Calcific degenerative disease is an active, inflammatory, osteogenic process — not simple wear and tear.
A bicuspid valve presents one to two decades earlier than a tricuspid valve.
Severe stenosis: valve area under 1.0 cm², mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more.
The onset of angina, syncope or heart failure marks a sharp fall in survival without intervention.
Angina occurs with normal coronary arteries because hypertrophy raises demand while perfusion pressure falls.
Low-flow, low-gradient stenosis can hide severe disease behind a deceptively low gradient.
There is no drug that stops progression — valve replacement is the treatment.

name: Aortic Regurgitation
tagline: Diastolic backflow from aorta to left ventricle, producing combined volume and pressure loading and a characteristically wide pulse pressure.
overview: Aortic regurgitation results either from disease of the cusps — bicuspid valve, rheumatic disease, endocarditis — or from dilatation of the aortic root that prevents the cusps meeting. Chronic regurgitation allows the ventricle to dilate and hypertrophy eccentrically over years, so patients remain asymptomatic for a long time and total stroke volume can be very large. Acute severe regurgitation, as in dissection or endocarditis, is entirely different: the non-dilated ventricle cannot accommodate the volume, filling pressures rise abruptly, and pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock develop rapidly.

modifiable: Hypertension, which accelerates root dilatation
Infective endocarditis risk factors
Untreated syphilis (historically important)
nonModifiable: Connective tissue disorders such as Marfan and Loeys–Dietz syndromes
Ankylosing spondylitis and other inflammatory aortitis

pathophysiology.title: Loss of cusp coaptation
pathophysiology.text: Cusp disease or annular and root dilatation prevents the cusps sealing in diastole, allowing blood to flow back into the ventricle.

pathophysiology.title: Volume overload
pathophysiology.text: The ventricle receives its normal transmitral filling plus the regurgitant volume, so end-diastolic volume rises substantially.

pathophysiology.title: Eccentric hypertrophy
pathophysiology.text: In chronic disease the ventricle adds sarcomeres in series, dilating while remaining relatively compliant. This accommodates the volume at acceptable filling pressures.

pathophysiology.title: Combined pressure load
pathophysiology.text: The large total stroke volume raises systolic pressure, so the ventricle faces both volume and pressure loading — a demanding combination.

pathophysiology.title: Wide pulse pressure
pathophysiology.text: High systolic pressure with a low diastolic pressure produces the wide pulse pressure and the many named peripheral signs of chronic aortic regurgitation.

pathophysiology.title: Coronary compromise
pathophysiology.text: Low aortic diastolic pressure reduces coronary perfusion pressure while hypertrophy raises demand, so angina can occur without coronary disease.

pathophysiology.title: Decompensation
pathophysiology.text: Progressive dilatation eventually exceeds compensatory capacity; contractility falls, ejection fraction declines and symptoms appear — often after irreversible myocardial change has begun.

anatomyInvolved: Aortic valve cusps and annulus
Aortic root and ascending aorta
Left ventricle, which dilates eccentrically
Coronary circulation, perfused at reduced diastolic pressure
physiologyChanges: Increased left ventricular end-diastolic volume and total stroke volume
Reduced effective forward stroke volume despite a large total output
Wide pulse pressure with low aortic diastolic pressure
Reduced coronary perfusion pressure
In acute regurgitation, an abrupt rise in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure with premature mitral valve closure

progression.text: Small regurgitant volume, normal ventricular dimensions, asymptomatic.
Marked ventricular dilatation with preserved ejection fraction; patients often remain asymptomatic for years.
Falling ejection fraction and rising end-systolic dimension, frequently preceding symptoms — which is why surveillance measurements matter.
A separate emergency: normal-sized ventricle, very high filling pressures, pulmonary oedema and shock.

symptoms: Long asymptomatic period in chronic disease
Exertional breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance
Palpitations and an uncomfortable awareness of the heartbeat
Angina, sometimes nocturnal
Rapid onset of severe breathlessness and collapse in acute regurgitation
signs: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge, best heard sitting forward in expiration
Collapsing (water-hammer) pulse and a wide pulse pressure
Displaced, hyperdynamic apex beat
Austin Flint murmur — a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex
Peripheral eponymous signs: Corrigan's, de Musset's, Quincke's, Traube's, Duroziez's and Müller's
In acute regurgitation: tachycardia, hypotension, a soft short murmur and pulmonary oedema — signs may be deceptively subtle

investigations.findings: Mechanism, regurgitant severity by multiple parameters, ventricular dimensions and function, and aortic root measurements.
Accurate regurgitant fraction and ventricular volumes; valuable when echocardiographic assessment is equivocal.
Aortic root and ascending aortic dimensions, essential where aortopathy is suspected.
Left ventricular hypertrophy with volume overload pattern in chronic disease.
Objective assessment of functional capacity in apparently asymptomatic patients.

complications: Progressive left ventricular dysfunction and heart failure
Aortic dissection where aortopathy is present
Sudden cardiac death, uncommon but recognised in severe disease

treatment.principles: Chronic severe regurgitation requires surveillance and timely surgery before irreversible ventricular damage occurs; the ventricular dimensions and ejection fraction are as important as symptoms. Acute severe regurgitation is a surgical emergency. Educational summary only.

groups.name: Surveillance
groups.detail: Serial echocardiography tracking ejection fraction and end-systolic dimension, with intervals set by severity.

groups.name: Medical therapy
groups.detail: Blood pressure control, particularly with vasodilating agents; beta-blockers and ARBs in aortopathy syndromes.

groups.name: Valve surgery
groups.detail: Aortic valve replacement, or repair and valve-sparing root replacement in selected anatomy and experienced centres.

groups.name: Root and ascending aortic surgery
groups.detail: Composite or valve-sparing root replacement when the aorta is dilated beyond threshold diameters.

groups.name: Acute management
groups.detail: Urgent surgery, with afterload reduction and inotropic support as a bridge. Intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation is contraindicated.

keyTakeaways: Caused either by cusp disease or by aortic root dilatation — always image the aorta.
Chronic disease is remarkably well tolerated because the ventricle dilates and stays compliant.
The wide pulse pressure explains the long list of peripheral eponymous signs.
Acute severe regurgitation is a different disease: a small stiff ventricle, pulmonary oedema and shock.
Ventricular dimensions and ejection fraction, not symptoms alone, drive the timing of surgery.

name: Mitral Stenosis
tagline: Obstruction to left ventricular filling at the mitral valve, overwhelmingly rheumatic in origin, raising left atrial pressure and causing pulmonary congestion.
overview: Mitral stenosis is almost always a late consequence of rheumatic fever, in which immune-mediated valvulitis causes commissural fusion, leaflet thickening and chordal shortening, producing the characteristic fish-mouth orifice. It remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity in many parts of the world. Because obstruction is upstream of the left ventricle, the ventricle itself is usually normal; the burden falls on the left atrium and, in time, the pulmonary vasculature and right heart. The diastolic gradient is exquisitely sensitive to heart rate, which is why patients often first decompensate with tachycardia — in exercise, pregnancy, fever or the onset of atrial fibrillation.

modifiable: Untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis
Crowded living conditions and limited access to healthcare
Non-adherence to secondary rheumatic fever prophylaxis
nonModifiable: Rarely: congenital mitral stenosis, severe annular calcification, radiation

pathophysiology.title: Rheumatic valvulitis
pathophysiology.text: Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac tissue provokes an immune response that damages the valve, often decades before symptoms appear.

pathophysiology.title: Commissural fusion and leaflet change
pathophysiology.text: Chronic inflammation fuses the commissures, thickens and calcifies leaflets and shortens chordae, progressively reducing the effective orifice.

pathophysiology.title: Transmitral gradient
pathophysiology.text: A diastolic pressure gradient develops between the left atrium and ventricle. Because the gradient depends on flow and on diastolic filling time, tachycardia sharply worsens it.

pathophysiology.title: Left atrial hypertension and dilatation
pathophysiology.text: Raised atrial pressure dilates the chamber and, transmitted backwards through valveless pulmonary veins, raises pulmonary capillary pressure and causes congestion.

pathophysiology.title: Pulmonary vascular change
pathophysiology.text: Sustained pulmonary venous hypertension causes reactive pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction and eventually fixed remodelling, producing pulmonary hypertension.

pathophysiology.title: Right heart consequences
pathophysiology.text: Right ventricular pressure overload leads to hypertrophy, dilatation, functional tricuspid regurgitation and right heart failure.

pathophysiology.title: Atrial fibrillation and thromboembolism
pathophysiology.text: Atrial dilatation and fibrosis promote atrial fibrillation, which both removes the atrial kick and greatly increases the risk of left atrial thrombus and systemic embolism.

anatomyInvolved: Mitral valve leaflets, commissures and subvalvular apparatus
Left atrium and its appendage
Pulmonary veins and pulmonary vasculature
Right ventricle and tricuspid valve
Left ventricle, typically normal or underfilled
physiologyChanges: Diastolic transmitral pressure gradient that rises steeply with heart rate
Elevated left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressures
Reduced left ventricular filling and fixed low cardiac output
Pulmonary hypertension, initially reactive and later fixed
Right ventricular pressure overload with secondary tricuspid regurgitation

progression.text: Years to decades between rheumatic fever and the appearance of symptoms.
Gradient appears with exertion; symptoms limited to exercise, pregnancy or febrile illness.
Valve area of about 1.5 cm² or less, with symptoms at rest or minimal exertion and pulmonary congestion.

progression.stage: Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure
progression.text: Fixed pulmonary vascular disease, tricuspid regurgitation, hepatic congestion, oedema and ascites.

symptoms: Exertional breathlessness, often first noticed during pregnancy or intercurrent illness
Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
Fatigue from a fixed low cardiac output
Palpitations with atrial fibrillation
Haemoptysis from ruptured bronchial veins
Hoarseness from left recurrent laryngeal nerve compression (Ortner's syndrome)
Embolic stroke as a presenting event
signs: Loud first heart sound with an opening snap after S2 — the shorter the S2–opening snap interval, the more severe the stenosis
Low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm, best heard in the left lateral position with the bell
Malar flush (mitral facies)
Tapping, non-displaced apex beat
Irregularly irregular pulse if in atrial fibrillation
Loud P2, right ventricular heave and raised JVP with pulmonary hypertension

investigations.findings: Valve area by planimetry and pressure half-time, mean gradient, leaflet morphology and mobility, left atrial size and pulmonary artery pressure.
Excludes left atrial appendage thrombus and assesses suitability for balloon valvuloplasty.
P mitrale — broad, notched P waves — in sinus rhythm; frequently atrial fibrillation; right ventricular hypertrophy with pulmonary hypertension.
Left atrial enlargement with a double right heart border and splayed carina, upper lobe venous diversion and Kerley B lines.
Assesses gradient and pulmonary pressure response when symptoms and resting findings disagree.

complications: Left atrial thrombus with systemic embolism and stroke
Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure

treatment.principles: Rate control protects diastolic filling time; anticoagulation is essential in atrial fibrillation, where vitamin K antagonists rather than direct oral anticoagulants are indicated in rheumatic mitral stenosis. Mechanical relief of obstruction is the definitive treatment, and percutaneous balloon commissurotomy is highly effective in suitable anatomy. Educational summary only.

groups.name: Rate control
groups.detail: Beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers to lengthen diastole and lower the gradient.

groups.name: Diuretics
groups.detail: For pulmonary congestion, used cautiously to avoid reducing an already limited preload.

groups.name: Anticoagulation
groups.detail: Warfarin for atrial fibrillation, prior embolism or left atrial thrombus in rheumatic mitral stenosis.

groups.name: Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy
groups.detail: First-line in suitable pliable valves without significant regurgitation or thrombus.

groups.name: Surgery
groups.detail: Open commissurotomy or mitral valve replacement when the anatomy is unsuitable for balloon therapy.

groups.name: Secondary prophylaxis
groups.detail: Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever in those with rheumatic heart disease.

keyTakeaways: Almost always rheumatic; commissural fusion produces the fish-mouth orifice.
The transmitral gradient depends on flow and diastolic time — tachycardia is what decompensates patients.
The left ventricle is usually normal; the burden falls on the left atrium and right heart.
Severe stenosis is defined by a valve area of about 1.5 cm² or less.
A shorter interval between S2 and the opening snap indicates more severe stenosis.
Rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation requires warfarin rather than a DOAC.

name: Mitral Regurgitation
tagline: Systolic backflow into the left atrium, from primary leaflet disease or secondary to ventricular remodelling — the commonest valve lesion overall.
overview: Mitral regurgitation is divided into primary disease, in which the valve apparatus itself is abnormal (most commonly myxomatous degeneration with prolapse, or chordal rupture, rheumatic disease or endocarditis), and secondary or functional disease, in which the leaflets are structurally normal but annular dilatation and papillary muscle displacement from ventricular remodelling prevent coaptation. The distinction is fundamental: primary disease is a valve problem treated by fixing the valve, whereas secondary disease is a ventricular problem in which treating the ventricle comes first. Chronic regurgitation is well tolerated for years; acute regurgitation, as from papillary muscle rupture, is a haemodynamic emergency.

modifiable: Ischaemic heart disease causing papillary muscle dysfunction
Hypertension and heart failure driving annular dilatation
Infective endocarditis risk factors
Untreated streptococcal infection in rheumatic disease
nonModifiable: Connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome
Genetic predisposition to mitral valve prolapse
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with systolic anterior motion

pathophysiology.title: Loss of coaptation
pathophysiology.text: Either the leaflets are abnormal (primary) or the apparatus is geometrically distorted by ventricular dilatation (secondary), so the valve fails to seal in systole.

pathophysiology.title: Regurgitant volume
pathophysiology.text: Part of the stroke volume is ejected backwards into the low-pressure left atrium. Because it ejects partly into a low-impedance chamber, the ventricle is initially unloaded and ejection fraction appears deceptively high.

pathophysiology.title: Left atrial volume overload
pathophysiology.text: The atrium receives both pulmonary venous return and the regurgitant volume. In chronic disease it dilates and remains compliant, so pressure rises only modestly.

pathophysiology.title: Left ventricular volume overload
pathophysiology.text: The whole regurgitant volume returns to the ventricle in diastole, causing eccentric hypertrophy and progressive dilatation.

pathophysiology.title: Vicious cycle in secondary disease
pathophysiology.text: Ventricular dilatation worsens regurgitation, which further volume-loads and dilates the ventricle — regurgitation begetting regurgitation.

pathophysiology.title: Progressive myocardial dysfunction
pathophysiology.text: Chronic volume overload eventually impairs contractility. Because the ventricle has been chronically unloaded, a 'normal' ejection fraction may already represent significant dysfunction.

pathophysiology.title: Acute regurgitation
pathophysiology.text: With sudden severe regurgitation, the small non-compliant atrium cannot accommodate the volume; atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise abruptly, causing flash pulmonary oedema and shock.

anatomyInvolved: Mitral leaflets, annulus, chordae tendineae and papillary muscles
Left atrium, which dilates in chronic disease
Left ventricle, volume-loaded and eccentrically hypertrophied
Pulmonary vasculature
Coronary supply to the posteromedial papillary muscle
physiologyChanges: Increased total stroke volume with reduced effective forward output
Left atrial volume overload with a prominent v wave
Left ventricular eccentric hypertrophy and dilatation
Deceptively preserved ejection fraction from chronic unloading
Elevated pulmonary venous pressures, abruptly so in acute disease

progression.text: Small regurgitant volume with normal chamber sizes and no symptoms.
Progressive left atrial and ventricular dilatation with preserved ejection fraction; often asymptomatic.
Rising end-systolic dimension and falling ejection fraction, frequently before symptoms — the reason for regular surveillance.
Sudden chordal or papillary muscle rupture with flash pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock.

symptoms: Long asymptomatic period in chronic disease
Exertional breathlessness and fatigue
Palpitations, often with atrial fibrillation
Orthopnoea and symptoms of heart failure as disease advances
Sudden severe breathlessness and collapse in acute regurgitation
signs: Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
Soft first heart sound; a third heart sound with significant volume overload
Displaced, hyperdynamic apex beat
Mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur in mitral valve prolapse
Signs of pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure in advanced disease
In acute regurgitation the murmur may be short or even absent — a dangerous pitfall

investigations.findings: Mechanism and severity by an integrated approach — effective regurgitant orifice area, regurgitant volume, vena contracta — plus chamber dimensions and function.
Segmental leaflet analysis (A1–A3, P1–P3) essential for surgical planning and procedural guidance.
Regurgitant volume and fraction, and accurate ventricular volumes; useful when echocardiography is discordant.
Left atrial enlargement, left ventricular hypertrophy, frequently atrial fibrillation.
Assesses dynamic severity and pulmonary pressures, particularly in secondary regurgitation.

complications: Progressive left ventricular dysfunction and heart failure
Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure
Sudden cardiac death in a small subset with prolapse and mitral annular disjunction

treatment.principles: In primary regurgitation, valve repair is preferred and is best performed before ventricular dysfunction develops. In secondary regurgitation, optimal guideline-directed heart failure therapy comes first, with transcatheter or surgical intervention considered when regurgitation remains severe and symptomatic. Educational summary only.

groups.name: Surveillance
groups.detail: Serial echocardiography tracking ejection fraction, end-systolic dimension and pulmonary pressures.

groups.name: Heart failure therapy
groups.detail: Foundational for secondary regurgitation — RAS inhibition, beta-blockade, MRA, SGLT2 inhibition and resynchronisation where indicated.

groups.name: Surgical repair
groups.detail: The preferred option in suitable degenerative disease, with better outcomes than replacement when durable repair is achievable.

groups.name: Valve replacement
groups.detail: When repair is not feasible, with preservation of the subvalvular apparatus where possible.

groups.name: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair
groups.detail: For selected patients at high surgical risk and for appropriately chosen secondary regurgitation.

groups.name: Acute management
groups.detail: Afterload reduction, mechanical support and urgent surgery for acute severe regurgitation.

keyTakeaways: Distinguish primary (valve) from secondary (ventricular) regurgitation — the treatment logic differs entirely.
A 'normal' ejection fraction may already indicate dysfunction, because the ventricle is chronically unloaded.
The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply and is the one that ruptures after infarction.
Chronic disease is well tolerated for years; acute disease causes flash pulmonary oedema and shock.
In acute severe regurgitation the murmur may be quiet or absent — never rely on murmur intensity.
Repair is preferred over replacement in suitable degenerative disease.

name: Tricuspid Regurgitation
tagline: Systolic backflow into the right atrium — usually secondary to right ventricular and annular dilatation, and increasingly recognised as prognostically important.
overview: Tricuspid regurgitation is common and, in trivial degrees, entirely normal. Clinically significant regurgitation is most often secondary or functional: the leaflets are structurally normal but the annulus has dilated and the papillary muscles have been displaced by right ventricular remodelling, usually driven by left heart disease or pulmonary hypertension. Primary disease — endocarditis, Ebstein's anomaly, carcinoid, trauma, or lead-related injury — accounts for a minority. Long dismissed as the 'forgotten valve', severe tricuspid regurgitation is now known to be independently associated with worse outcomes, and transcatheter therapies are developing rapidly.

modifiable: Left heart disease raising pulmonary pressures
Pulmonary hypertension of any cause
Atrial fibrillation with atrial and annular dilatation
Intracardiac device leads crossing the valve
Injection drug use predisposing to endocarditis
nonModifiable: Ebstein's anomaly and other congenital lesions

pathophysiology.title: Right ventricular pressure or volume overload
pathophysiology.text: Left heart disease, pulmonary hypertension or intrinsic right ventricular disease causes the ventricle to dilate.

pathophysiology.title: Annular dilatation
pathophysiology.text: The non-planar tricuspid annulus dilates, predominantly along its free wall, increasing the distance the leaflets must cover to coapt.

pathophysiology.title: Leaflet tethering
pathophysiology.text: Papillary muscle displacement from ventricular remodelling tethers the leaflets apically, further reducing coaptation.

pathophysiology.title: Regurgitant volume and atrial overload
pathophysiology.text: Systolic backflow raises right atrial pressure, producing a giant v wave and transmitting pressure into the systemic veins.

pathophysiology.title: Self-perpetuating cycle
pathophysiology.text: Volume overload dilates the right ventricle further, worsening annular dilatation and tethering — regurgitation begetting regurgitation.

pathophysiology.title: Systemic venous congestion
pathophysiology.text: Sustained venous hypertension produces hepatic congestion, ascites, oedema and, eventually, cardiac cirrhosis and renal dysfunction.

anatomyInvolved: Tricuspid annulus, leaflets and subvalvular apparatus
Right ventricle and its papillary muscles
Right atrium, which dilates markedly
Systemic veins, liver and kidneys
physiologyChanges: Reduced effective forward flow into the pulmonary circulation
Elevated right atrial pressure with a giant v wave in the jugular venous pulse
Progressive right ventricular volume overload and dilatation
Systemic venous congestion with hepatic and renal consequences
Reduced left ventricular preload and therefore reduced cardiac output

progression.text: Detected in most normal hearts on echocardiography; of no clinical significance.
Annular dilatation from right ventricular remodelling; usually asymptomatic.
Marked annular dilatation with leaflet tethering, giant v waves and systemic congestion.
Right ventricular failure, cardiac cirrhosis, refractory ascites and renal dysfunction; intervention carries high risk at this point.

symptoms: Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance from low forward output
Abdominal swelling and discomfort from ascites and hepatic congestion
Peripheral oedema
Early satiety and anorexia
Pulsation in the neck and, sometimes, the liver
signs: Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge increasing on inspiration (Carvallo's sign)
Giant v waves in the jugular venous pulse
Pulsatile, tender hepatomegaly
Ascites and dependent pitting oedema
Left parasternal heave from right ventricular dilatation
Jaundice and signs of chronic hepatic congestion in advanced disease

investigations.findings: Severity grading, annular diameter, leaflet tethering, right ventricular size and function, and estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure.
Accurate assessment of the non-planar annulus and coaptation gap, essential for transcatheter planning.
Reference standard for right ventricular volumes, function and regurgitant fraction.
Pulmonary pressures and resistance, distinguishing regurgitation driven by pulmonary hypertension from isolated disease.
Liver function, hepatic elastography and renal function to quantify end-organ consequences.

complications: Reduced survival independent of other cardiac disease

treatment.principles: Treat the underlying driver — left heart disease, pulmonary hypertension or arrhythmia — before considering the valve. Diuretics relieve congestion. Concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty at the time of left-sided surgery prevents late deterioration, and transcatheter options are expanding for patients unsuitable for surgery. Educational summary only.

groups.name: Treat the underlying cause
groups.detail: Optimising left heart failure therapy, treating pulmonary hypertension and restoring sinus rhythm where feasible.

groups.name: Diuretics
groups.detail: Loop diuretics with aldosterone antagonists for systemic congestion and ascites.

groups.name: Surgical annuloplasty
groups.detail: Performed at the time of left-sided valve surgery when the annulus is dilated, even if regurgitation is only moderate.

groups.name: Tricuspid valve replacement
groups.detail: For primary disease not amenable to repair; carries higher operative risk.

groups.name: Transcatheter therapy
groups.detail: Edge-to-edge repair, annuloplasty devices and transcatheter replacement in selected high-risk patients.

groups.name: Lead management
groups.detail: Careful consideration of lead position, extraction or leadless alternatives in lead-induced regurgitation.

keyTakeaways: Most clinically significant tricuspid regurgitation is secondary to right ventricular and annular dilatation.
Giant v waves and pulsatile hepatomegaly are the classic bedside findings.
Right-sided murmurs increase on inspiration — Carvallo's sign.
It is not benign: severe regurgitation independently predicts worse outcomes.
Always look for and treat the underlying left heart or pulmonary cause first.
Intervening before right ventricular and hepatic decompensation gives far better results.
